transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’ve been having trouble when people are talking to me. Like at the museum, someone will be telling me about the next art walk, and I’m looking right at them, but then I realize I missed a chunk of what they said. I end up having to ask them to repeat it.
Do you think you weren't paying attention when you missed what they said, or did you just not understand it?

I think it’s more that I’m not staying with it, even though I’m looking right at them. I usually understand them fine, but somewhere in the middle I just miss part of what they said, and then I have to ask them to go over it again.
Do you find that this happens with all kinds of conversations, or just in certain situations or environments?

It’s most noticeable in situations like at the museum, when someone’s talking right to me about the next art walk or something like that. I’ll be looking at them and trying to listen, but then I realize I missed the middle part and I have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you have trouble following conversations when there's background noise?

I notice it mostly at the museum when someone’s talking right to me about something like the next art walk. I’m looking at them, and I think I’m listening, but then I realize I missed the middle of what they said and I have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you think you're actually hearing the words but not processing them, or do you think you're just not hearing the words at all when you miss part of what someone says?

I think I’m hearing them at first, but I’m not really taking it all in. Like at the museum, someone will be talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’ll be looking at them, but then I realize I missed the middle part and have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you have trouble following conversations when there's no background noise?

Yes, it can happen even without much noise. Like I said, someone at the museum can be talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’m looking at them, but I’ll still miss the middle of what they said and need them to repeat it.
Do you have trouble understanding what people are saying, or is it more that you forget what they said after they've finished talking?

It’s more that I don’t really take in the middle of what they’re saying while they’re talking. I’m looking at them, and I hear them start, but then afterward I realize I missed a chunk of it. So I have to ask them to say it again, like when people at the museum are telling me about the next art walk.
Do you have trouble understanding what people are saying immediately after they say it, or is it more that you can't recall what they said a little while later?

It’s more immediate, I think. Like, they’ll finish saying it and I realize I didn’t catch the middle part, even though I was looking at them. At the museum, someone might be explaining the next art walk, and I have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you think you would have an easier time following what someone is saying if they wrote it down for you to read?

I think so, yes. If it’s written down, I can look back at it. When someone at the museum is just telling me about the next art walk, even if I’m looking right at them, I might miss the middle of it and have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you think you would be able to follow and understand a conversation better if someone spoke more slowly to you?

Maybe a little, but I’m not sure it’s really about speed. It’s more like they’ll be talking right to me, like at the museum about the next art walk, and I’m looking at them, but then I realize I missed the middle of it. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you have trouble understanding what people are saying when they use complex sentences or complicated vocabulary?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed it being about big words or complicated sentences. It’s more just… sometimes I don’t catch what was said right away.
Do you have trouble understanding what people are saying when they talk to you in a quiet room with no distractions?

Yes, it can still happen even if it’s quiet. That’s kind of what brings me in—someone at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’m looking at them, but then I realize I missed the middle of what they said. So I end up asking them to run it by me again.
Do you think you would be able to repeat back what someone just said to you, right after they finish talking?

Sometimes I can repeat part of it, but not all of it. Like at the museum, someone will be telling me about the next art walk, and I’m looking right at them, but then I realize I missed the middle. So if they asked me to repeat it back, I’d probably have to ask them to run it by me again.
Do you have trouble understanding speech when it's presented in a way that doesn't allow you to see the speaker's lips or face?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed if it’s specifically worse when I can’t see someone’s face or lips. I’d have to pay attention to that.
Do you think you have a harder time understanding what someone is saying when you're not looking at them, like when you're talking on the phone?
I’m not sure. I use the phone some, but I haven’t really noticed whether it’s harder because I’m not looking at the person. I’d have to pay closer attention to that.
Do you think you would have an easier time understanding what someone is saying if you couldn't see their face or lips while they are talking?
I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed that not seeing someone’s face or lips makes it easier for me. I’d say I’m just not sure either way.
Do you think you would have an easier or harder time understanding what someone is saying if you were talking to them in a completely dark room?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really been in that situation enough to say if a dark room would make it easier or harder. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear difference.
Do you think you would be able to understand what someone is saying if they spoke in very short sentences?

I think short sentences would probably help some. The problem I notice is more when someone’s talking to me, like at the museum about the next art walk, and I’m looking right at them, but I still miss the middle of what they said. Then I have to ask them to say it again. So if it’s kept short, I’d probably follow it better.
Do you think you would be able to understand what someone is saying if they spoke in your native language, but with a very strong accent?

I’m not really sure. I think a very strong accent might make it harder for me, but I haven’t noticed a consistent problem one way or the other. It would probably depend on the person and how clearly they were speaking.
Do you think you would be able to understand what someone is saying if they spoke very clearly and at a normal pace, but used made-up words that you had never heard before?

I’m not sure about that. If they were made-up words I’d probably be confused, even if they were speaking clearly. I guess I’d understand the regular parts of the sentence, but not know what those new words meant.
